editorial_contributions.text: By assigning one of two given colors to every point of the plane, we get a 2-colored plane. It is well known (and easily proved) that in any 2-colored plane there are two points of the same color 1 apart. I decided to look into the existence of larger than 2-point sets. The problem of finding the smallest number of colors needed to color all the points in the plane in such a way that no color realizes all distances, meaning that for every color used there exists a positive number \(d\) such that no two points of that color have distance \(d\), is a celebrated open problem due to Paul Erdős. Raiskii, at the time a high school student in Moscow, proved that \(\chi_p \geq 4\) [\textit{D. E. Rajskij}, Math. Notes 7, 194--196 (1970; Zbl 0202.21702), translation from Mat. Zametki 7, 319--323 (1970; Zbl 0191.20506)]. 


 The author of this article presents a proof of the above lower bound given by another high school student in Moscow, Alexei Merkov, in 1997. The proof is indeed quite beautiful and worth reading. For a history of this problem as well as related coloring problems see [\textit{A. Soifer}, The mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. New York, NY: Springer (2009; Zbl 1221.05001)].

editorial_contributions.text: This paper describes the life of the mathematician Issai Schur (1875--1941) and his pioneering contributions to Ramsey theory. Probably the best-known result due to Schur says that given a positive integer \(k\), there is a positive integer \(N\) such that if the set \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) is partitioned into \(k\) classes, then one of the classes contains numbers \(a\) and \(b\) together with their sum \(a+b\). This result was published in 1916 [Deutsche Math. Ver. 25, 114--117 (1916; JFM 46.0193.02)] and Schur obtained it when working on a certain number-theoretic problem. Although some authors in the past claimed that Schur never devoted himself to similar problems again, the current paper explains that this was not the case. For example, Schur deserves the credit for conjecturing the monochromatic arithmetic sequences theorem proved in 1927 by \textit{B. L. van der Waerden} [Abhandlungen Hamburg 5, 185--187 (1927; JFM 53.0171.02)] (given a pair of positive integers \(k\) and \(n\), there is a positive integer \(N\) such that if the set \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\) is partitioned into \(k\) classes, then one of the classes contains an arithmetic progression of length \(n\)). Soon after this proof, Schur arrived at a statement which generalizes both his 1916 theorem and Van der Waerden's theorem. Schur has also influenced his students, who have later discovered other important Ramseyan results. As the author remarks, ``Issai Schur had been the most instrumental leader in the development of Ramsey Theory before Ramsey.''

Let \(G\) be the infinite graph whose vertices are the points of the plane and whose edges connect vertices of Euclidean distance 1. An open problem is to determine the chromatic number of \(G\). By a theorem of Erdős the chromatic number of this infinite graph is equal to the maximum chromatic number of its finite subgraphs. It is known that the number is between 4 (by giving a specific subgraph requiring 4 colors) and 7 (by giving a proper coloring of all points in the plane). The large gap between the bounds is part of this problem's appeal.

In this expository paper the author examines the history of this problem. It has been attributed to a number of different proposers, as have the above mentioned bounds.

Given an \(n\)-coloring of the plane such that the color \(i\) does not realise the distance \(d_i\) \((1 \leq i \leq n)\), we say that this coloring has type \((d_1, d_2, \dots, d_n)\). In 1992 [J. By our former results mentioned above we have \(1/ \sqrt 5\), \(\sqrt 2 - 1 \in\text{X}_6\). In this note we prove the following result: \([\sqrt 2 - 1,1/ \sqrt 5] \subseteq \text{X}_6\), i.e., for every \(\alpha \in [\sqrt 2 - 1, 1/ \sqrt 5]\) there is a 6-coloring of type \((1,1,1,1,1, \alpha)\).

editorial_contributions.text: The article sketches the life of the famous German algebraist, Issai Schur (1875-1941), until his dismissal from the University of Berlin by the racist laws of the Nazis in 1935. The paper then tries to solve the `mystery', raised by L. Mirsky, why Schur never returned to combinatorics which he had entered via his classic lemma on partitions of integers in 1916, ``which gave birth (in the opinion of the author) ... to a new direction in mathematics; now called Ramsey Theory.'' L. van der Waerden in 1926. The author supports Brauers assertion, partly using biographical material on Baudet which was provided to him by the Dutch historian of mathematics, Gerard Alberts. The question whether Baudet created the conjecture independently remains open.

editorial_contributions.text: This article looks into the origins of the conjecture proven by Bartel L. van der Waerden, now known as van der Waerden's theorem (in Ramsey Theory). Although van der Waerden himself credited Pierre J. H. Baudet with the conjecture, some have credited Issai Schur. The article asserts the following. Alfred Brauer gave a talk in 1960 in which he said that Schur had made the conjecture as a ``helpful lemma'' towards two conjectures on quadratic residues. (This account is consistent with the memories of Paul Erdős and Brauer's brother Richard, and with second-hand information from Erich Rothe.) The date that Schur made the conjecture is unclear from the article, exept that it was ``many years'' before van der Waerden proved it in 1927. Baudet was a ``brilliant young Ph. D.'' and chessplayer who died young in 1921. He was a protege of Frederick Schuh; van der Waerden suggests that he picked up the conjecture at ``one of the (monthly) meetings of the Wiskundig Genootschap, where Schuh appeared regularly''. The article presents two scenarios. First, Baudet may have developed the conjecture independently and passed it to Schuh, who passed it on to van der Waerden. Second, Baudet may have got the conjecture from Schur, perhaps directly when Baudet visited Berlin in 1921, who passed it on to Schuh, etc. The article concludes by proposing that van der Waerden's Theorem also be remembered as the Baudet-Schur Conjecture.

This very nicely presented book, lovingly prepared by the author over a period of 18 years, studies problems involving colored objects, and the Ramsey theory that such problems are imbedded into. ``This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation, trains of mathematical thought, and where possible, psychology of mathematical invention. The book does not just include history and prehistory of Ramsey theory and related fields, but also conveys the process of historical investigation -- the kitchen of historical research if you will. It has captivated me, and made me feel like a Sherlock Holmes -- I hope my reader will enjoy this sense of suspense and discovery as much as I have. \dots I hope the book will present mathematics as a human endeavor: the reader should expect to find in it not only results, but also portraits of their creators; not only mathematical facts, but also open problems; not only new mathematical research, but also new historical investigations; not only mathematical aspirations, but also moral dilemmas of the times between and during the two horrific World Wars of the twentieth century.''


 
For example, new facts and artifacts are presented, pertaining to the lives of Issai Schur, Pierre Joseph Henry Baudet, and Bartel Leendert van der Waerden. The 49 chapters are divided into 11 parts: I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps (a map is defined to be a plane connected multigraph with no bridges); V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principle; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of chromatic number of the plane; X. Predicting the future (here the author conjectures that the chromatic number of the plane is either 4 or 7, expressing a preference for 7); XI. Farewell to the reader. There are an extensive bibliography, and indices of names, subjects, and notations; the latter two are brief. The author has used his own book as a text, at both the senior and the graduate level. There are numerous open problems, but no formal problem sets. But there is much to recommend this book, both for mathematicians and for those who wish to learn more about mathematicians and their subject.

For any given cardinal \(\lambda\) a group G is said to be \(\lambda\)- decomposable if for every \(\sigma <\lambda\), G decomposes into a direct sum of \(\sigma\) non-zero summands. A group which is not \(\lambda\)- decomposable is said to be \(\lambda\)-indecomposable. After having defined what is meant by a group passing the infinite test, the so-called infinite test lemma is proved: 


Let G be a group of singular cardinality of cofinality \(\omega\). Then G is \(| G|\) \(+\)-indecomposable only if it passes the infinite test. Furthermore the infinite test is also sufficient for \(| G|\) \(+\)- indecomposability, if G satisfies any one of the following conditions: (*) \(| G/T(G)| <| G|\), (**) G is quasi-\(\sigma\)-separable for some \(\sigma <| G|\), i.e. every summand of G contains a summand of cardinality less than \(\sigma\). 


The author then proves the main result: Let G be an abelian group of singular cardinality \(\lambda\) of cofinality \(\omega\), satisfying one of the conditions (*) or (**). If G is \(\lambda\)-decomposable, then G is \(\lambda\) \(+\)-decomposable. The author conjectures: In singular cardinality \(\lambda\), \(\lambda\)-decomposable groups are \(\lambda\) \(+\)- decomposable.

editorial_contributions.text:
Chromatic graph theory deals with coloring vertices, edges, or both of a graph \(G\) according to certain simple rules. However, the simplicity of the rules does not mean that the problems encountered are simple. Starting from the four-color problem around 1850, the theory has developed into a many-sided body of problems, theories, results, and applications. The number of simply stated but challenging problems remains large and growing.

The author's Mathematical coloring book (TMCB) was published in 2009 [The mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. Forewords by Branko Grünbaum, Peter D. Johnson jun., and Cecil Rousseau. New York, NY: Springer (2009; Zbl 1221.05001)]. It is now joined by the New mathematical coloring book (TNMCB), which is a colossal sibling of TMCB. This second edition of the book is a masterpiece, containing more than twice as much as the first edition. It includes striking results from the past fifteen years and solutions to problems from the first edition.

This very nicely presented book studies problems involving colored objects and the Ramsey theory. It mainly deals with the four-color problem and the author's favorite problem, namely, the chromatic number of the plane problem: What is the smallest number of colors needed for coloring the points of the plane in such a way that any two points at distance one receive two different colors? This book includes not just mathematics, but also the process of investigation. It is a unique combination of mathematics, history, and biography and the author has been intimately involved in the story for the last half-century. Mathematics is presented both as science and art and the author has set a standard for writing about mathematics and mathematicians that will be hard to match. The author engages the reader's attention not only mathematically, but emotionally and esthetically.

TNMCB consists of 68 chapters divided into 14 parts. I. Merry-go-round; II. Colored plane; III. Coloring graphs; IV. Coloring maps; V. Colored graphs; VI. The Ramsey principles; VII. Colored integers: Ramsey theory before Ramsey and its aftermath; VIII. Colored polygons: Euclidean Ramsey theory; IX. Colored integers in service of the chromatic number of the plane: how O'Donnell unified Ramsey theory and no one noticed; X. Ask what your computer can do for you XI. What about chromatic 6?; XII. Predicting the future; XIII. Imagining the real and realizing the imaginary; XIV. Farewell to the reader.

A large part of this new edition presents the most recent works by Auberg de Grey, Marijn Heule, Jann Parts, Geoffrey Exoo, and Don Ismailescu. New open problems and conjectures are included and this will lead to further work on the theme of this book. This book is strongly recommended to all those who wish to learn more about mathematics, mathematicians, the process of investigation and the psychology of mathematical invention.

After recalling the proofs by E. Nelson (1950) and J. editorial_contributions.text: An abelian group G is \(\aleph_ 0\)-indecomposable if G cannot be written as a direct sum of \(\aleph_ 0\) non-zero groups. A convenient but interesting reformulation of the \(\aleph_ 0\)-decomposability for a reduced countable mixed group G with finite torsion-free rank is that every finite subset can be imbedded in a summand of finite index. editorial_contributions.text: Shelah and Soifer have shown the remarkable fact that the chromatic number of some graphs depends on which axioms are assumed for the underlying set theory. For the purpose of this review, such graphs will be called SS-graphs. This short note explores the idea of SS-graphs, although there is little here that was not in the second author's earlier papers. Again the graphs under consideration have the points of Euclidean space as vertices, with two vertices adjacent if the distance between them lies in a given set \(D\) of distances. The main result is that in one dimension there are `as many' choices of \(D\) which produce an SS-graph as there are choices of \(D\) that produce a non SS-graph. (For both cases, the number of choices is the cardinality of the power set of the reals). On the basis of this (perhaps flimsy) evidence, the authors conjecture that for any uncountable cardinal \(\alpha\), among graphs with at most \(\alpha\) vertices there are as many SS-graphs as there are non-SS graphs.

editorial_contributions.text: A group is \(\aleph_ 0\)-indecomposable if it cannot be decomposed into a direct sum of \(\aleph_ 0\) non-zero summands. In this paper the authors find necessary and sufficient conditions for an extension of a countable reduced torsion abelian group T by a finite rank torsion-free abelian group R to be \(\aleph_ 0\)-indecomposable. These conditions are remarkably simple, and depend only on T and R: Let R have rank n and Richman type the matrix t. Then T has a basic subgroup which decomposes as a direct sum of \(n+1\) summands \(B_ 0,B_ 1,...,B_ n\) such that \(B_ 0\) is finite; for \(i\geq 1\), \(B_ i\) has no two adjacent non-zero Ulm-Kaplansky invariants; and for \(i\geq 1\) and all primes p, \([r_{pi}]\leq t\), where \(r_{pi}\) is the p-rank of \(B_ i\).

editorial_contributions.text: Given a colouring of (all the points of) the plane with colours \(1,2, \dots, n\), the colour \(i\) is said to forbid, or not to realize, the distance \(d_i\) if no two points in the plane separated by (Euclidean) distance \(d_i\) are of colour \(i\). An \(n\)-colouring of the plane is said to be of type \((d_1, \dots, d_n)\) if for each \(i\), \(1 \leq i \leq n\), the colour \(i\) forbids the distance \(d_i\). The almost chromatic number of the plane \(\chi_a\) is the minimum number \(n\) such that a colouring of type \((1, \dots, 1, d_n)\) exists for some \(d_n\). In [\textit{A. Soifer}, A six-coloring of the plane, J. Comb. Theory, Ser. A 61, No. 2, 292-294 (1992; Zbl 0756.05057)] the inequality \(\chi_a \leq 6\) was proved by exhibiting a 6-coloring of type \((1,1,1, 1, 1,1/ \sqrt 5)\). The present paper exhibits a 6-colouring of type \((1,1,1,1,1, \sqrt 2 - 1)\). The paper contains an error which is corrected in [\textit{I. Hoffman} and \textit{A. Soifer}, Correction for: Almost chromatic number of the plane, Geombinatorics 3, No. 3, 102 (1994; Zbl 0845.05038 below)].

editorial_contributions.text:
In the second edition of an engagingly written book [see Zbl 0691.52001 , ME 1991h.02126 for the first edition], addressed to bright high school students and undergraduates, whose contributions are very nicely incorporated into the narrative, the author presents problems belonging to discrete and combinatorial geometry. It starts by solving the problem of (1) finding all positive integers \(n\) for which every triangle can be cut into \(n\) triangles similar to each other (all \(n\neq 2, 3, 5\)), and the problem of (2) finding all positive integers \(n\) for which every triangle can be cut into \(n\) triangles congruent to each other (all \(n = k^2\), for some \(k\geq 1\)). It then moves on to provide two proofs for the fact that (3) of any five points in a triangle of unit area there are three that form a triangle of area \(\leq \frac{1}{4}\). 

R. Peng showed in 1989, while a senior high school student, that \(\leq \frac{1}{4}\) can be replaced in (3) with \(\leq (\sqrt{2}-1)^2\), and that this is the best possible constant. With \(S_{\alpha}(F)\) defined as the minimal positive integer \(n\) such that among any \(n\) points located inside or on the boundary of the figure \(F\), there are three points which form a triangle of area at most \(\alpha \cdot |F|\) where \(|F|\) denotes the area of \(F\), the author shows that \(S_{\frac{1}{4}}(F)\) must be 5 or 6 for all convex figures \(F\), and that both 5 and 6 occur (5 whenever \(F\) is a triangle, and 6 when \(F\) is a regular pentagon).

Among the many Erdős conjectures to be found in this book, we mention two: (4) That, among all triangles formed by three of the vertices of any convex pentagon of unit area, one must have an area of at most \(\frac{5-\sqrt{5}}{10}\), and that this bound (attained in the case of the regular pentagon) is best possible; (5) Find the smallest and the largest value of \(\alpha\) such that for every convex figure \(F\), \(S_{\alpha}(F)\) is 5 or 6.

A second part was added to this second edition, on developments since the publication of the first edition (1990). It contains another proof of (1), several results by M. Laczkovicz on cutting triangles, the result of the collaboration of the author with J. H. Conway, regarding the number of unit equilateral triangles it takes to cover an equilateral triangle of side \(n + \varepsilon\) (\(n^2 + 2\) unit equilateral triangles suffice, and it is conjectured that \(n^2 + 1\) do not suffice). Somewhat confusingly, it also contains M. Kahle's improvement of \(\leq \frac{1}{4}\) in (3) to \(\leq \frac{6}{25}\) and his conjecture that the best possible constant in (3) is \(\frac{1}{6}\) (although the matter had been settled by Peng's result, and the conjecture disproved).

However, Kahle's involvement with the problem fits nicely with the overall message of the book, that elementary mathematics fascinates those who have encountered it while they were in high school long after their Olympiad experiences are over. Kahle had encountered (3) on one of his five attendances of the Colorado Mathematical Olympiad (called into life and run for 26 years by the author) in 1988, and provided the improved bound 20 years later -- while a Postdoctoral Fellow at Stanford. The fact that Kahle, a two time gold medalist of the Colorado Mathematical Olympiad, had not been admitted to the University of Colorado at Colorado Springs for grade point average reasons speaks eloquently about both the ineptitude of the admission rules and regulations and the irrelevance of the institution of high school mathematics in the United States of America (which is, at best, concerned with questions of the kind ``prove that \(A\) implies \(B\) using the Pythagorean theorem'' (Preface, xxix)), and leaves graduates ``without the foggiest idea of what mathematics is'' (Preface, xxviii), as the latter assigned Kahle a grade of C in geometry.

editorial_contributions.text:
Bartel Leendert van der Waerden was a prolific and influential mathematician of the twentieth century -- through textbooks, research, and editorial activity, esp.\ for the \textit{Mathematische Annalen} -- as well as a writer on the history of science in Antiquity. He chose to stay on his chair at Leipzig University throughout the Nazi era, which then created major problems for him in his home country, the Netherlands, after the war. His life and work clearly deserve thorough historical study. The book under review presents a valuable, lavishly illustrated piece of investigative journalism with quite a bit of new (at least to the reviewer) information and evidence about van der Waerden's life; but only one tiny gem from van der Waerden's vast and rich mathematics is discussed (in Chapters 7, 37, and 38). Several of the findings had already been described by the author in his earlier book [The mathematical coloring book. Mathematics of coloring and the colorful life of its creators. New York, NY: Springer (2009; Zbl 1221.05001)] and other earlier publications. The author unfortunately does either not cite, or barely mentions relevant studies like [\textit{R. Siegmund-Schultze}, ``Bartel Leendert van der Waerden (1903--1996) im Dritten Reich: Moderne Algebra im Dienste des Anti-Modernismus?'', in: B. Hoffmann (ed.) and M. Walker (ed.), `Fremde' Wissenschaftler im Dritten Reich. Göttingen: Wallstein (2011)] (along with other important chapters of that same book), [the reviewer, ``A historical sketch of B. L. van der Waerden's work in algebraic geometry: 1926--1946'', in: Episodes in the history of modern algebra (1800--1950). Based on a workshop held at MSRI, Berkeley, CA, USA, April 2003. Providence, RI: American Mathematical Society (AMS); London: London Mathematical Society. 245--283 (2007; Zbl 1129.01012)], or [\textit{M. R. Schneider}, Zwischen zwei Disziplinen. B. L. van der Waerden und die Entwicklung der Quantenmechanik. Berlin: Springer (2011; Zbl 1233.01009)], even though his presentation could have profited from taking them into account. 

Perhaps the most striking novel elements in the book include information about van der Waerden's Dutch family and upbringing, as well as his fate after 1945, including the remarkable story of Rolf Nevanlinna's and van der Waerden's hiring at the University of Zürich (Chapters 25, 26, 30, and 39). Van der Waerden's stance with respect to the Nazi regime is often discussed in parallel to Werner Heisenberg's attitude and with considerable moral emphasis (Chapters 15, 32, 33, 34). Indeed, Heisenberg was one of van der Waerden's colleagues in Leipzig before the war, and the author appropriately points to their close correspondence after the war, which includes a defense strategy for Heisenberg developed by van der Waerden. 

Anybody seriously interested in van der Waerden has to take this rich and detailed book into account. At the same time it may be regretted that a book about ``the scholar and the state'' never asks how politics may have affected the content or presentation of van der Waerden's mathematics. When such an influence actually suggests itself in Chapter 9, where van der Waerden's famous suppression of the axiom of choice from the 1937 edition of his well-known algebra book is discussed, the author describes this as a ``victory of Brouwer's intuitionism'', and he is then puzzled to see that van der Waerden reverted back to his original treatment in 1950, when times have changed. Also, when the author discusses his favourite mathematical theorem of van der Waerden, his historical questions hardly go beyond priority issues for conjectures or results. In [Zbl 1129.01012], I have tried to show how political agendas entered van der Waerden's favourite domain of research, algebraic geometry. Also, van der Waerden's forays into statistics constitute a fertile ground for genuine history of mathematics. And the political undercurrents of van der Waerden's work on the history of mathematics call for closer inspection. None of this is touched upon in the book under review. 
 
The author, even though he calls himself a historian, deliberately adopts a journalistic style, sharing with the reader his personal adventure through a great number of archival documents, his astonishments and personal reactions, as well as some of the exchanges with people who provided him with information. The journalistic character of the text shows rather crudely when written and oral sources are treated indiscriminately; for example on p.\ 186, the author reproduces a fairly unlikely interpretation transmitted by Washnitzer of something Helmut Hasse had said at the Oslo ICM in 1936, even though there is absolutely no shortage of written, archived documents showing very precisely how well Hasse arranged himself with the Nazi regime, while at the same time keeping his distance from the ``Deutsche Mathematik'' in Bieberbach's and Teichmüller's way. Here and elsewhere the author tends to work with an oversimplified picture of the Nazi regime. For example on p.\ 99 he exclaims with respect to Richard Courant's having to leave Germany even though he had been a frontline fighter in WWI: ``Doesn't this episode clearly illustrate the lawlessness of the new Third Reich?'' Now, it is true that the law of 7 April 1933 was never applied to Courant who finally resigned from his position in 1934, following Hasse's suggestion. But the author's rhetorical question underestimates the cunning interplay of the various clauses written into the law. Those who made this law knew very well how to exert \textit{legal} pressure: the exception for frontline fighters applied to \S3 (dismissal of non-Aryans), but not for example to \S4 (political incompatibility), and even less to the general arbitrary clause \S6 (administrative simplification). This is why those who in 1933 or 1934 wrote petitions for Courant or for Edmund Landau (who had not fought in the war, but was exempt from \S3 because he had been a professor already before WWI) typically tried to argue with a view to \S4 that these Jews protected from \S3 were also politically inoffensive. Contrary to the author, van der Waerden did appreciate these distinctions, for instance in his letter of support for Edmund Landau of 6 February 1934 (which the author does not quote directly). Explaining such details could have benefited the author's account (Chapter 15) of van der Waerden's and Heisenberg's protest at the 1935 faculty meeting in Leipzig. 
 
Journalistic is also the way in which the author at times tries to enter into van der Waerden's (or Heisenberg's) mind, whereas at other times he just lays out pieces of evidence for the reader to interpret, but arranging them in a way that seems to want to suggest a conclusion which, however, is not explicitly stated. See for instance the anti-chronological order in which events are told in Chapter 13 on the 1933 offer from the IAS, Princeton, which van der Waerden finally turned down even though he had received official authorisation to accept it. 
 
On the technical level, there are of course occasional oversights which are inevitable in a book of this size; for instance, the name of the physicist James Franck is misspelled on p.\ 91; and p.\ 224 and p.\ 279 contradict each other about whether the Queen's own opinion did or did not matter for approving the appointment of a professor at any Dutch university. Troublesome, however, is the fact that the author is not a reliable translator of his German sources, and has not had his translations checked sufficiently carefully by others. This poses a real problem for using the book as a basis for further work, since the original texts of most of the sources are unfortunately not supplied; maybe this could still be done on the internet? To quote just one non-trivial instance of this recurrent problem, on p.\ 116, where the translation misses the scene described: it is of course not Geyer who ``forbade Professor Golf to speak in the tone he was using'', but rather Golf who reprimands van der Waerden for raising his voice (the translation confuses \textit{verbitten} and \textit{verbieten}, and thus fails to interpolate the missing `s' in front of \textit{ich}).

The authors consider one known combinatoric problem connected with colorings of grids. They say that any \(k\)-coloring of vertices of \(G\) is \(k\)-complete, if for every pair of different colors \(i,j\in[k]\), \(i \neq j\), there exists an edge \(\{u,v\}\) in \(G\) such that \(u\) is assigned to \(i\) while \(v\) is assigned to \(j\). They are interested in maximizing \(k\). In the case when the coloring is proper, the problem reduces to the very well-known problem of \(a\)-coloring. 

The authors prove that every grid of size \(n \times n\), \(2 \leq n \leq 8\), demands \(2n-1\) colors to be complete colorable. Some lower bounds on the number \(k\) is given for bigger grids. I find the most valuable in the paper the giving of some tools/useful lemmas that can lead to improve known results. It seems that some improvements in the topic are feasible.

editorial_contributions.text:
This is a popular book written for talented high school students. Also a mathematician can get much pleasure in recalling some well known theorems and problems on tilings, graphs, and most of all on convex figures. Very many exercises with solutions are built into the text. This gives some extra pleasure to the reader and enables to draw him into an active study. 


The following fragment of the introduction by Branko Grünbaum is worth mentioning: ``Mathematics in general, and geometry in particular, are fields in which the small amount of formal instruction given in schools is not sufficient to bring latent talents to full development. Individual work and effort are necessary.... The present book is an appealing step in the direction of providing useful supplementary reading and practice material.''


Chapter 1. Tiling a checker rectangle (64 pages), concerns tilings with trominoes, tetrominoes and polyominoes. 


Chapter 2. Proofs of existence (25 pages), says mainly on the Bolzano- Weierstrass theorem and on the isoperimetric problem. 


Chapter 3. Graphs (46 pages), deals with the Ramsey number, planar graphs and, surprisingly, with the Jordan theorem. 


Chapter 4. Ideas and combinatorial geometry (90 pages), concerns combinatorial aspects of convexity. Most attention is paid to figures of constant width, to the Borsuk's partition problem, to the Hadwiger's covering problem, and to the theorems of Helly and Szökefalvi-Nagy.


 In many places the book is similar to some fragments of earlier books coauthored by the first author and scientific articles of the second author listed in the Bibliography. Particularly we have in mind the book of \textit{I. M. Yaglom} and the first author [Convex figures (1961; Zbl 0098.35501)] and the book of the first author and \textit{I. Ts. Gohberg} [Results and problems in combinatorial geometry (1985; Zbl 0567.52007)].
